title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical team reference for on-call engineers, runtime maintainers, and performance engineers. Read this before making changes to scheduling kernels, batching heuristics, or deployment topology.

Sections
- Runtime architecture overview
- Kernel scheduling and placement strategies
- Profiling playbook (how-to)
- Benchmarking suite: workloads and expected outputs
- Release notes (rolling 6 months)
- Known issues and mitigations
- Runtime runbooks: incidents and maintenance procedures
- Team wiki and links

1) Runtime architecture overview

Short intro
The serving runtime is a high-throughput inference engine designed to serve autoregressive and encoder-decoder models with low latency and predictable throughput. The runtime composes three logical layers: Frontend Router, Execution Runtime (kernels + scheduler), and Cache/State Store.

Components
- Frontend Router: API surface, request validation, auth, rate limiting, and route-based policy (latency-first / cost-first).
- Scheduler: sits between frontend and kernel pool, responsible for batching decisions, kernel selection, and placement across GPUs/hosts.
- Kernel Pool / Execution Engines: model-specific optimized kernels (fused attention, rotary/ALiBi variants, quantized kernels). Each kernel exposes a stable runtime API.
- KV/Prefix Cache: per-model/tenant prefix cache for hot prompts and shared KV cache for multi-tenant reuse.
- Metrics & Tracing: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and token-level cost instrumentation.

Architecture diagram (text)
Frontend Router --> Scheduler (batching + placement) --> Kernel Pool (GPU workers)
                                      
Cache <------------------------------------------------^
Metrics / Tracing / Rollouts (control plane) run alongside and feed runtime tuning pipelines.

SLOs & targets (summary table)
| Metric | Target |
|--------|--------|
| P95 latency (1–64 tokens) | <= 45ms |
| P99 latency (1–64 tokens) | <= 120ms |
| Availability (Serving control plane) | 99.95% |
| Token throughput per-GPU (BERT-like seq256) | baseline published per model in model-catalog |

Ownership and escalation
- Runtime core: eng-serving-runtime (oncall alias: eng-runtime-oncall)
- Kernel library: eng-serving-runtime-kernels
- Observability/alerts: eng-sre

2) Kernel scheduling and placement strategies

Goals
- Maximize aggregated throughput while meeting latency SLOs for latency-sensitive routes.
- Efficiently utilize memory for KV cache and quantized models.
- Provide graceful degradation (fallback to CPU or lower-capacity model variant) on overload.

Policies and heuristics
- Route policy annotations: each route is tagged with latency_priority: high|medium|low and cost_policy: aggressive|balanced|conservative. Scheduler respects latency_priority first.
- Kernel selection table (priority):
  1. Native fused kernel (preferred for large batches, low-latency fused attention)
  2. Quantized kernel (4-bit / 8-bit) for cost-sensitive requests
  3. Compatibility kernel (slower but supports unsupported ops)
- Affinity and anti-affinity: tenant-affinity is enabled by default for Dedicated customers; multi-tenant pooling uses soft-affinity to reduce cold KV misses.
- Batching windows: adaptive based on observed p50 inter-arrival time. Initial window default: 2ms; max window: 12ms (configurable per-deployment).

Placement rules
- Prefer colocating kernel + KV cache on same host to avoid cross-host fetches for prefixes > 2kB.
- For large seq-length requests (>1024 tokens), schedule to hosts with ephemeral memory headroom >= 20%.
- Use host-level load score = (gpu_util * 0.6) + (pending_batches * 0.4) to choose placement; threshold for spillover: > 0.75.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Purpose: run consistent, low-noise profiles to identify kernel hotspots, memory fragmentation, and scheduler decisions causing tail latency.

Prerequisites
- Access to profiling cluster (label: profiling=true).
- Profiling image: runtime-profiling:stable.
- Flamegraph tooling: speedscope / pyflame / Nsight (GPU kernels).

Step-by-step
1. Prepare a representative workload: use the benchmark harness (see section 4) to capture request mix and token lengths.
2. Isolate the node: cordon the node and drain non-profiling traffic.
3. Start system-level collection: collect nvidia-smi -lms 500 for 60s, capture dmesg and /proc/zoneinfo.
4. Start tracing in runtime: set env RUNTIME_TRACE_LEVEL=kernel, RUNTIME_BATCH_TRACE=1 for a 5–10 minute window.
5. Run the benchmark workload with --trace-sample-rate=0.05 to conserve space (tooling will correlate traces with batch ids).
6. Collect kernel-level profiles: run nvprof / nsight for 2–4 representative batches, capture kernel latency distribution.
7. Aggregate traces: use the profiling aggregator (cli: profiling-agg --input traces/* --output profile-report.html).
8. Analyze results:
   - Look for heavy skew in batch construction time vs kernel execution time.
   - Check for frequent 'cold start' kernel loads (kernel init > 30ms).
   - Verify KV cache hit rate (target >= 60% for production routes).
9. Action: open a tracking issue with labels runtime/perf and assign to the responsible kernel owner. Include aggregate graphs and a prioritized list of changes (e.g., kernel fusion, operator scheduling, cache eviction tuning).

Quick commands
- Start trace on node: kubectl exec -n runtime -it runtime-agent -- sh -c "RUNTIME_TRACE=1 RUNTIME_BATCH_TRACE=1 /bin/start-trace"
- Collect nvprof: nvprof --print-gpu-trace -o nvprof.out --profile-child-processes <command>

4) Benchmarking suite: workloads and expected outputs

Overview
The benchmarking suite is in infra/benchmarks/serving-harness. It supports: latency-only synthetic workloads, production-replay (captures), and mixed (PLG) mixes that simulate real traffic patterns. Benchmarks are reproducible via container images.

Workloads
- synth-short: 1–64 tokens, 70% short completion, 30% mid-length prompts
- synth-long: 512–2048 tokens, used for stress tests and memory checks
- replay-prod: scrubbed production replay for route-specific benchmarking (requires sec approval)
- embeddings-bulk: batched embedding workloads for throughput tuning

How to run (example)
1. Checkout: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-harness.git
2. Build: make docker-build
3. Run (latency profile):
   docker run --rm -e TARGET_URL=https://runtime.staging.redwood.internal:8443 \
     serving-harness:latest run --profile synth-short --concurrency 64 --duration 600

Expected outputs (sample)
- CSV metrics: p50,p95,p99,throughput,tokens_per_sec
- JSON trace samples (correlated to batch ids)
- artifacts: flamegraphs/, nvprof/

Acceptance criteria for changes to scheduler or kernels
- No regression in p99 latency > 5% for latency-priority routes on synth-short after tuning.
- Throughput improvement >= 8% is considered significant if latency SLOs are unimpaired.

Benchmark config table
| Flag | Default | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| --concurrency | 32 | number of parallel clients |
| --duration | 300s | benchmark runtime |
| --trace-sample-rate | 0.01 | fraction of requests traced |

5) Release notes (recent, rolling 6 months)

2027-02-28: Runtime v2.14.0 (stable)
- Improvements: fused attention kernel for decoder-only models reduced mean token latency by 18% for synth-short.
- New: adaptive batching window enabled by default in staging (2ms -> 8ms adaptive).
- Fix: resolved KV cache eviction bug causing cold misses under burst.

2026-11-12: Runtime v2.12.3 (patch)
- Patch: fixed a race in kernel library initialization that caused rare OOM on heterogeneous GPU hosts.
- Observability: added token-level cost metrics.

2026-08-03: Runtime v2.10.0
- Feature: quantized 4-bit kernels for gpt-3 style models. Reduced VRAM by ~40% in lab tests.

6) Known issues and mitigations

Issue: P99 spikes during load tests with mixed short/long workloads
- Symptom: p99 latency spikes up to 350ms when long requests arrive interleaved with short.
- Root cause: scheduler favors batching; long requests block batch formation and increase tail for short requests.
- Mitigation: enable route-level latency_priority=high to carve out a low-latency fast-path (scheduler will preempt long requests). Temporary workaround: set batching_window_max=6ms for affected nodes.

Issue: KV cache fragmentation on long-lived hosts
- Symptom: degraded cache hit rate over weeks, memory churn.
- Mitigation: periodic cache compaction job (cron: cache-compact --host <host> --threshold 0.2). Rotation policy: restart host weekly in low-traffic window.

Issue: Cross-host prefix fetches on Dedicated causing 20% extra latency
- Mitigation: prefer colocated cache placement for Dedicated customers; if not possible, advertise upstream hints to pre-warm remote KV. Measurement: trace upstream fetches; aim for <5% cross-host fetches.

7) Runtime runbooks (incidents and maintenance procedures)

Incident: Elevated p99 on production route
1. Triage: check Grafana dashboard "runtime/latency-by-route" and the recent change log.
2. Isolate: confirm if traffic pattern changed (use request-sampler service) or a deploy happened.
3. Quick mitigation: toggle route policy to latency_priority=high or reduce batching_window_max to 4ms for the route.
4. If mitigation fails: scale up kernel pool (k8s hpa: replicas +2 for affected node pool) and divert new requests to fallback region.
5. Post-incident: run profiling playbook and open a postmortem.

Maintenance: kernel library upgrade checklist
1. Validate unit tests and kernel-level microbenchmarks on staging.
2. Run end-to-end benchmarks (synth-short, synth-long) and compare to baseline.
3. Canary rollout: 5% traffic for 2 hours, monitor p95/p99 and GPU OOM counters.
4. If canary passes, rollout incrementally (5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%) with 30–60 minute observation windows.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: runtime-scheduler-config
data:
  batching_window_ms: "6"
  max_batch_size: "128"
  latency_priority_window_ms: "2"
  host_load_threshold: "0.75"

Appendix: example profiling-agg command
profiling-agg --input /tmp/traces --output /tmp/profile-report.html --model gpt-4x --top-n-kernels 20

Document change control
- Major changes to scheduling heuristics or kernel libraries must be reviewed by eng-serving-runtime and eng-sre. Submit a PR with benchmark artifacts, regression charts, and a rollback plan.
